issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

A second session that arrives in the container root with a request that is a subtask of an open campaign — while another session on this machine already holds that campaign — is today told to "join" it, which makes it a second campaign session: it surveys, files, claims, launches, and may sync or close the anchor. Witnessed 2026-08-28: session `agent-workspace-51` filed and claimed #36 while `agent-workspace-3a` (the session running campaign #1) sat idle and learned nothing, because nothing in `AGENTS.md`, `opening-campaign`, or the protocol says a session can be an *executor*. The holding session can see the peer in `ListAgents` (liveness) but cannot tell which subtask it works or address it for STATUS, so its close gate and its retirement sweep are blind to it — the "several sessions × the protocol" gap named in #36.

The rule to add, and where it lands:

1. **AGENTS.md § Who is a campaign session.** A session whose request is a subtask of an open campaign, when `ListAgents` shows a peer session on this machine, becomes that subtask's **executor session**: it files the subtask (or takes the one it was given), claims the branch, announces the claim to the holding session, and from then on is an agent in the protocol — it answers STATUS, sends REPORT and BLOCKED, stops on STAND DOWN, and never surveys, syncs, or closes the anchor. The holding session is the peer the person named; when none was named, the announcement goes to every peer session and a peer that holds no campaign covering it ignores it. The executor keeps working the subtask the way any executor may (own hands, subagent on a worktree, or a delegate); what changes is only who it reports to.
2. **The protocol gains one message**, executor → campaign, sent once at claim: `CLAIMED <branch> <ListAgents name>`. It carries only what the executor alone knows — its address — because the branch and the issue are already GitHub facts and the name of an interactive session cannot be set to the branch after launch (the `--name`-is-the-branch rule covers launched delegates only; probe whether a running session can rename itself and, if it can, make renaming to the flattened branch the first step and keep CLAIMED for the holding session's benefit). Update the four-message table in AGENTS.md § Talking to a repository agent and the protocol's header in `spec/alloy/agent.als`.
3. **Liveness for an executor session is a `ListAgents` fact**, read the same way `herdr agent

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`closing-campaign` step 5 releases every `campaign-<N>/` ref still sitting at
`origin/main`, and it reads them with

```sh
gh api "repos/kalaluthien/agent-workspace/git/matching-refs/heads/campaign-$N/"
```

with **no `--paginate`**. GitHub pages that endpoint at thirty, so a campaign
with more than thirty branches gets a truncated list — and a truncated list of
refs reads exactly like a complete one, which is the sentence `AGENTS.md` already
uses about the sub-issue index two hundred lines earlier.

The consequence is quiet rather than destructive: refs past the first page are
never released, so claims outlive their campaign and the next campaign meets
branches nobody can explain. Nothing errors and the close reports success.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, which bounded five `gh issue list` surveys
on the same argument. This is the same class in the one place that reads refs
rather than issues, and it was not in #65's scope.

The work: add `--paginate`, and check whether any other `gh api` call in the two
skills or in `scripts/` reads a paged endpoint without it. `AGENTS.md:434`,
`opening-campaign/SKILL.md:332`, `docs/campaign-lifecycle.html:209` and
`scripts/campaign-settlement:86` were all verified paginated on 2026-08-30, so
the sweep is small.

Done when the pull request is merged, and the sweep's result is stated — the
fixed call, plus the list of `gh api` calls checked and found already correct.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`AGENTS.md` will say, once #65 lands, that **liveness has one reader**,
`scripts/campaign-session-alive`, and that the comparison must never be
hand-rolled. Nothing enforces it.

This repository's own rule, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` § Design: *a declared contract
stays true only while a second reader enforces it, a validator or hook on the
authoring side. With the consumer as its only reader, the contract drifts exactly
like the hardcoded copy it replaced.* The four hand-rolled copies #65 removes are
what that drift looks like when it has already happened — they were four prose
copies of one test, and they were all wrong together.

Verified 2026-08-30: nothing under `spec/` or `docs/` mentions
`campaign-session-alive`; the only "one reader" sentence in `spec/` is
`ledger.als:27`, about `alloy-check`.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#61

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`
plan_items: `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.
issue.title: Name a session campaign-<anchor>-<role>-<n>, and retire the branch-as-name rule

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#61

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`

`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

## What is wrong

`campaign-1/80-phase2-sweep` (#80, PR #94) adds a third merge condition — the branch contains the current `main` at the moment it merges. Its chain survives attack. **Nothing enforces it.**

The owner authorised branch protection on `main` to fix that, and it was applied:

```
required_status_checks: { strict: true, contexts: [] }
enforce_admins: true
allow_force_pushes: false
allow_deletions: false
```

**Measured, and it enforces nothing.** A throwaway branch one commit behind `main` (#96, closed and deleted) read `mergeable=MERGEABLE`, `mergeStateStatus=CLEAN`, twice several seconds apart, with `behind=1 ahead=1`. "Require branches to be up to date" is a *modifier on required status checks*, and with `contexts: []` there is nothing for it to modify. The setting stores, reads back `strict=true`, and does nothing.

That is a sharper fact than an absent setting, and it is exactly the failure this campaign keeps meeting: a claimed reader that does not read. The force-push and deletion blocks **are** real.

## The work

Add one GitHub Actions workflow running the checks this repository already owns, and register it as a required status check so `strict` has something to be strict about.

- `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.
- `scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

**Ordering matters and is the part to get right.** A required check that no open pull request can produce blocks every merge. So: land the workflow first, watch it run green on a real pull request, and only then add its context to `required_status_checks.contexts`. Two pull requests are open while this lands.

Second-order benefit, and arguably the larger one: the guard and the model stop depending on a person remembering to run them. Today `alloy-check` is run because a rule says to.

## Done when

The pull request is merged, the workflow has run green on it, `contexts` names it, and a branch deliberately left behind `main` is refused — demonstrated the same way the current setting was falsified, not argued from the settings page.
plan_items: `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.

`scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

Observed 2026-09-02 on #116: the stood-down delegate (`campaign-116-executor-1`), asked by the owner what was left, read `campaign-tracker settlement 116`, saw #119 `open`, and offered to take it — while `campaign-116-executor-2` was already running its `rm -rf`. No double execution happened (the offer was never accepted), but the only thing that prevented it was the owner not saying yes.

## Five whys

Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

#176 made the branch ref the whole claim. That works for one repository and one shape of sub-issue. Four questions it left open were found by review on PR #183 (rounds three and four) and are deferred here rather than fixed there, because they are one design and not four fixes: PR #183's own record is that fixing them piecemeal produced a new stratum of defects each round.

Absorbs #186, which is question 1 stated narrowly.

## The design, before any code

Each of these gets a rule in `spec/campaign/` with a scenario that reddens when the rule is removed, and only then a script change.

**1. Claim identity across repositories.** `Claimed` is a set over `Issue`, so the model says a claim is per sub-issue. The script keys it by branch NAME and reads a repository list derived from the clones on disk, which gives three defects at once: `take` sweeps and re-checks on `--repo` only, so two takers with different `--repo` both claim the same sub-issue; `all_refs` collapses a same-named ref in a second repository, so `release` can delete the wrong one; and a member repository named in `## Repos` but not cloned here is unread while `live` prints that all readings were made. Decide what a claim's identity IS — the sub-issue, the (repository, branch) pair, or the sub-issue's own `repo` field — and make the readers agree with the model.

Also here, from PR #184's audit (N2): the model reads a claim over `claimedIssues` and has no `checkedOut` derivation, so a prunable-worktree scenario cannot discriminate from `R4h`. Whatever identity this question settles, derive the worktree reading (`checkedOut`) from it in the model, or record why the model stops above it.

**2. Release and close for a sub-issue whose ref never gains a commit.** `take --local` is gone, so a sub-issue whose work lives only under `<campaign>/scripts/` cuts a ref that stays level with `main`. `release` then refuses it as indistinguishable from a fresh claim, `--confirmed-absent` would be a false statement, and `closing-campaign` step 1 refuses on it. `spec/campaign/session/scenarios.als`'s `R4_RepolessCampaign` says exactly this campaign closes; the script at #183's head says it cannot. Campaign: kalaluthien/campaign-base#1
Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

An executor that has just merged a sub-issue carries that sub-issue's whole transcript, and every turn of the next sub-issue re-reads it. `/compact` is the one thing that shrinks it, and nothing sends it. Two owner corrections on 2026-09-05 shaped what lands: compaction must fire the instant the executor is done, while that context is still in the prompt cache — run later it re-reads the whole transcript uncached and costs more than it saves; and the first draft's planner-side protocol and claim-ordering rule were too complex. One mechanism, at one moment.

Second: `AGENTS.md` states two channels in two sections with no criterion between them — § Delegate launch says a first brief arrives by `herdr agent prompt`, § The four messages says STATUS/REPORT/BLOCKED/STAND DOWN travel between sessions. A later assignment to a reused executor, the answer to a BLOCKED, and a slash command are undefined. That criterion belongs with this handoff, because both halves are the one handoff.

## What lands

1. **`campaign-claim.py release` enqueues `/compact` into the releasing session's own pane**, as its last act: `HERDR_ENV=1 herdr agent prompt <own pane> "/compact"`. herdr queues a prompt against a working pane, so compaction fires the moment the release turn ends, on the context that turn just used. The script finds its own pane by joining its harness session id to `herdr agent list`, and prints what it read — session id, pane, the command sent. **When no row names this session it says so and releases anyway**: compaction is a cost rule, not a gate, and a missing row must be visible, never silent. It never prompts a pane that is not its own.
2. **`scripts/campaign-assign.py <pane> <sub-issue>` is the planner's only assignment path.** It checks the pane is idle and has compacted since its last release — reading the pane text for the compaction marker, could-not-look printed and never silent — then sends the one-sentence prompt naming the sub-issue.
3. **The channel rule, stated once**, as one paragraph in `AGENTS.md` § The four messages naming that script: *an instruction to a session is a prompt into its pane; information between sessions is one of the four messages.* So every assignment (first or later), the answer to a BLOCKED, and `/compact` are prompts; REPORT, BLOCKED, STATUS and STAND DOWN stay messages. label.rule: file of the merged PR that closed the sub-issue

issue.definition_of_done:
- A session reading a large file is steered to a grep and a bounded range by something it must consume, not a third copy of the prose.
- A review subagent's diff read is exempt.
- The threshold and the exemption are each stated once, and the check prints what it read and which branch it took.
- A case for each outcome fails first, then passes: steered, exempt, small file.
- The prose copies point at the check, or go.
issue.intent:
- rule-check#429 measured reads at 35.5% of tool-result bytes (rule-check#412). Its option C, grep first and then a bounded range, served:
  - 7 of 7 runs at 9.1% of the bytes (experiment 4, issuecomment-5660485351);
  - 6 of 6 anchored runs at 2.3% (experiment 5, issuecomment-5660796247).
- Review reads scored lower, but every miss lay outside the text read, so a whole read would have missed them too.
- The owner, 2026-09-14: make C the rule for a session's reads, and keep review diffs read whole.
- The rule exists in prose already: `AGENTS.md` § Execution mode says "Read only the part of a file you need", and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` says so too. The bytes show it is not followed, so the prose alone does not hold.
plan_items: First a `NOTE` with options, each tied to the #429 numbers and judged by bytes saved and wrong answers risked:
a `PreToolUse` hook on `Read` with no range over N lines;
a line in the brief hook;
a `filing`-shaped rule in `~/.claude/`;
others.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

A second session that arrives in the container root with a request that is a subtask of an open campaign — while another session on this machine already holds that campaign — is today told to "join" it, which makes it a second campaign session: it surveys, files, claims, launches, and may sync or close the anchor. Witnessed 2026-08-28: session `agent-workspace-51` filed and claimed #36 while `agent-workspace-3a` (the session running campaign #1) sat idle and learned nothing, because nothing in `AGENTS.md`, `opening-campaign`, or the protocol says a session can be an *executor*. The holding session can see the peer in `ListAgents` (liveness) but cannot tell which subtask it works or address it for STATUS, so its close gate and its retirement sweep are blind to it — the "several sessions × the protocol" gap named in #36.

The rule to add, and where it lands:

1. **AGENTS.md § Who is a campaign session.** A session whose request is a subtask of an open campaign, when `ListAgents` shows a peer session on this machine, becomes that subtask's **executor session**: it files the subtask (or takes the one it was given), claims the branch, announces the claim to the holding session, and from then on is an agent in the protocol — it answers STATUS, sends REPORT and BLOCKED, stops on STAND DOWN, and never surveys, syncs, or closes the anchor. The holding session is the peer the person named; when none was named, the announcement goes to every peer session and a peer that holds no campaign covering it ignores it. The executor keeps working the subtask the way any executor may (own hands, subagent on a worktree, or a delegate); what changes is only who it reports to.
2. **The protocol gains one message**, executor → campaign, sent once at claim: `CLAIMED <branch> <ListAgents name>`. It carries only what the executor alone knows — its address — because the branch and the issue are already GitHub facts and the name of an interactive session cannot be set to the branch after launch (the `--name`-is-the-branch rule covers launched delegates only; probe whether a running session can rename itself and, if it can, make renaming to the flattened branch the first step and keep CLAIMED for the holding session's benefit). Update the four-message table in AGENTS.md § Talking to a repository agent and the protocol's header in `spec/alloy/agent.als`.
3. **Liveness for an executor session is a `ListAgents` fact**, read the same way `herdr agent

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`closing-campaign` step 5 releases every `campaign-<N>/` ref still sitting at
`origin/main`, and it reads them with

```sh
gh api "repos/kalaluthien/agent-workspace/git/matching-refs/heads/campaign-$N/"
```

with **no `--paginate`**. GitHub pages that endpoint at thirty, so a campaign
with more than thirty branches gets a truncated list — and a truncated list of
refs reads exactly like a complete one, which is the sentence `AGENTS.md` already
uses about the sub-issue index two hundred lines earlier.

The consequence is quiet rather than destructive: refs past the first page are
never released, so claims outlive their campaign and the next campaign meets
branches nobody can explain. Nothing errors and the close reports success.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, which bounded five `gh issue list` surveys
on the same argument. This is the same class in the one place that reads refs
rather than issues, and it was not in #65's scope.

The work: add `--paginate`, and check whether any other `gh api` call in the two
skills or in `scripts/` reads a paged endpoint without it. `AGENTS.md:434`,
`opening-campaign/SKILL.md:332`, `docs/campaign-lifecycle.html:209` and
`scripts/campaign-settlement:86` were all verified paginated on 2026-08-30, so
the sweep is small.

Done when the pull request is merged, and the sweep's result is stated — the
fixed call, plus the list of `gh api` calls checked and found already correct.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`AGENTS.md` will say, once #65 lands, that **liveness has one reader**,
`scripts/campaign-session-alive`, and that the comparison must never be

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#61

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`
plan_items: `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.
issue.title: Name a session campaign-<anchor>-<role>-<n>, and retire the branch-as-name rule

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

## What is wrong

`campaign-1/80-phase2-sweep` (#80, PR #94) adds a third merge condition — the branch contains the current `main` at the moment it merges. Its chain survives attack. **Nothing enforces it.**

The owner authorised branch protection on `main` to fix that, and it was applied:

```
required_status_checks: { strict: true, contexts: [] }
enforce_admins: true
allow_force_pushes: false
allow_deletions: false
```

**Measured, and it enforces nothing.** A throwaway branch one commit behind `main` (#96, closed and deleted) read `mergeable=MERGEABLE`, `mergeStateStatus=CLEAN`, twice several seconds apart, with `behind=1 ahead=1`. "Require branches to be up to date" is a *modifier on required status checks*, and with `contexts: []` there is nothing for it to modify. The setting stores, reads back `strict=true`, and does nothing.

That is a sharper fact than an absent setting, and it is exactly the failure this campaign keeps meeting: a claimed reader that does not read. The force-push and deletion blocks **are** real.

## The work

Add one GitHub Actions workflow running the checks this repository already owns, and register it as a required status check so `strict` has something to be strict about.

- `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.
- `scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

**Ordering matters and is the part to get right.** A required check that no open pull request can produce blocks every merge. So: land the workflow first, watch it run green on a real pull request, and only then add its context to `required_status_checks.contexts`. Two pull requests are open while this lands.

Second-order benefit, and arguably the larger one: the guard and the model stop depending on a person remembering to run them. Today `alloy-check` is run because a rule says to.

## Done when

The pull request is merged, the workflow has run green on it, `contexts` names it, and a branch deliberately left behind `main` is refused — demonstrated the same way the current setting was falsified, not argued from the settings page.

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

Observed 2026-09-02 on #116: the stood-down delegate (`campaign-116-executor-1`), asked by the owner what was left, read `campaign-tracker settlement 116`, saw #119 `open`, and offered to take it — while `campaign-116-executor-2` was already running its `rm -rf`. Absorbs #186, which is question 1 stated narrowly.

## The design, before any code

Each of these gets a rule in `spec/campaign/` with a scenario that reddens when the rule is removed, and only then a script change.

**1. Claim identity across repositories.** `Claimed` is a set over `Issue`, so the model says a claim is per sub-issue. The script keys it by branch NAME and reads a repository list derived from the clones on disk, which gives three defects at once: `take` sweeps and re-checks on `--repo` only, so two takers with different `--repo` both claim the same sub-issue; `all_refs` collapses a same-named ref in a second repository, so `release` can delete the wrong one; and a member repository named in `## Repos` but not cloned here is unread while `live` prints that all readings were made. Decide what a claim's identity IS — the sub-issue, the (repository, branch) pair, or the sub-issue's own `repo` field — and make the readers agree with the model.

Whatever identity this question settles, derive the worktree reading (`checkedOut`) from it in the model, or record why the model stops above it.

Campaign: kalaluthien/campaign-base#1
Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

An executor that has just merged a sub-issue carries that sub-issue's whole transcript, and every turn of the next sub-issue re-reads it. `/compact` is the one thing that shrinks it, and nothing sends it. Two owner corrections on 2026-09-05 shaped what lands: compaction must fire the instant the executor is done, while that context is still in the prompt cache — run later it re-reads the whole transcript uncached and costs more than it saves; and the first draft's planner-side protocol and claim-ordering rule were too complex. One mechanism, at one moment.

Second: `AGENTS.md` states two channels in two sections with no criterion between them — § Delegate launch says a first brief arrives by `herdr agent prompt`, § The four messages says STATUS/REPORT/BLOCKED/STAND DOWN travel between sessions. A later assignment to a reused executor, the answer to a BLOCKED, and a slash command are undefined. That criterion belongs with this handoff, because both halves are the one handoff.

## What lands

1. **`campaign-claim.py release` enqueues `/compact` into the releasing session's own pane**, as its last act: `HERDR_ENV=1 herdr agent prompt <own pane> "/compact"`. herdr queues a prompt against a working pane, so compaction fires the moment the release turn ends, on the context that turn just used. The script finds its own pane by joining its harness session id to `herdr agent list`, and prints what it read — session id, pane, the command sent. **When no row names this session it says so and releases anyway**: compaction is a cost rule, not a gate, and a missing row must be visible, never silent. It never prompts a pane that is not its own.
2. **`scripts/campaign-assign.py <pane> <sub-issue>` is the planner's only assignment path.** It checks the pane is idle and has compacted since its last release — reading the pane text for the compaction marker, could-not-look printed and never silent — then sends the one-sentence prompt naming the sub-issue.
3. **The channel rule, stated once**, as one paragraph in `AGENTS.md` § The four messages naming that script: *an instruction to a session is a prompt into its pane; information between sessions is one of the four messages.* So every assignment (first or later), the answer to a BLOCKED, and `/compact` are prompts; REPORT, BLOCKED, STATUS and STAND DOWN stay messages. label.rule: file of the merged PR that closed the sub-issue

issue.definition_of_done:
- A session reading a large file is steered to a grep and a bounded range by something it must consume, not a third copy of the prose.
- A review subagent's diff read is exempt.
- The threshold and the exemption are each stated once, and the check prints what it read and which branch it took.
- A case for each outcome fails first, then passes: steered, exempt, small file.
- The prose copies point at the check, or go.
issue.intent:
- rule-check#429 measured reads at 35.5% of tool-result bytes (rule-check#412). Its option C, grep first and then a bounded range, served:
  - 7 of 7 runs at 9.1% of the bytes (experiment 4, issuecomment-5660485351);
  - 6 of 6 anchored runs at 2.3% (experiment 5, issuecomment-5660796247).
- Review reads scored lower, but every miss lay outside the text read, so a whole read would have missed them too.
- The owner, 2026-09-14: make C the rule for a session's reads, and keep review diffs read whole.
- The rule exists in prose already: `AGENTS.md` § Execution mode says "Read only the part of a file you need", and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` says so too. The bytes show it is not followed, so the prose alone does not hold.
plan_items: First a `NOTE` with options, each tied to the #429 numbers and judged by bytes saved and wrong answers risked:
a `PreToolUse` hook on `Read` with no range over N lines;
a line in the brief hook;
a `filing`-shaped rule in `~/.claude/`;
others.

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

A second session that arrives in the container root with a request that is a subtask of an open campaign — while another session on this machine already holds that campaign — is today told to "join" it, which makes it a second campaign session: it surveys, files, claims, launches, and may sync or close the anchor. Witnessed 2026-08-28: session `agent-workspace-51` filed and claimed #36 while `agent-workspace-3a` (the session running campaign #1) sat idle and learned nothing, because nothing in `AGENTS.md`, `opening-campaign`, or the protocol says a session can be an *executor*. The holding session can see the peer in `ListAgents` (liveness) but cannot tell which subtask it works or address it for STATUS, so its close gate and its retirement sweep are blind to it — the "several sessions × the protocol" gap named in #36.

The rule to add, and where it lands:

1. **AGENTS.md § Who is a campaign session.** A session whose request is a subtask of an open campaign, when `ListAgents` shows a peer session on this machine, becomes that subtask's **executor session**: it files the subtask (or takes the one it was given), claims the branch, announces the claim to the holding session, and from then on is an agent in the protocol — it answers STATUS, sends REPORT and BLOCKED, stops on STAND DOWN, and never surveys, syncs, or closes the anchor. The holding session is the peer the person named; when none was named, the announcement goes to every peer session and a peer that holds no campaign covering it ignores it. The executor keeps working the subtask the way any executor may (own hands, subagent on a worktree, or a delegate); what changes is only who it reports to.
2. **The protocol gains one message**, executor → campaign, sent once at claim: `CLAIMED <branch> <ListAgents name>`. issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`closing-campaign` step 5 releases every `campaign-<N>/` ref still sitting at
`origin/main`, and it reads them with

```sh
gh api "repos/kalaluthien/agent-workspace/git/matching-refs/heads/campaign-$N/"
```

with **no `--paginate`**. GitHub pages that endpoint at thirty, so a campaign
with more than thirty branches gets a truncated list — and a truncated list of
refs reads exactly like a complete one, which is the sentence `AGENTS.md` already
uses about the sub-issue index two hundred lines earlier.

The consequence is quiet rather than destructive: refs past the first page are
never released, so claims outlive their campaign and the next campaign meets
branches nobody can explain. Nothing errors and the close reports success.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, which bounded five `gh issue list` surveys
on the same argument. This is the same class in the one place that reads refs
rather than issues, and it was not in #65's scope.

The work: add `--paginate`, and check whether any other `gh api` call in the two
skills or in `scripts/` reads a paged endpoint without it. `AGENTS.md:434`,
`opening-campaign/SKILL.md:332`, `docs/campaign-lifecycle.html:209` and
`scripts/campaign-settlement:86` were all verified paginated on 2026-08-30, so
the sweep is small.

Done when the pull request is merged, and the sweep's result is stated — the
fixed call, plus the list of `gh api` calls checked and found already correct.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`AGENTS.md` will say, once #65 lands, that **liveness has one reader**,
`scripts/campaign-session-alive`, and that the comparison must never be
hand-rolled. Nothing enforces it.

This repository's own rule, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` § Design: *a declared contract
stays true only while a second reader enforces it, a validator or hook on the
authoring side. With the consumer as its only reader, the contract drifts exactly
like the hardcoded copy it replaced.* The four hand-rolled copies #65 removes are
what that drift looks like when it has already happened — they were four prose
copies of one test, and they were all wrong together.

Verified 2026-08-30: nothing under `spec/` or `docs/` mentions
`campaign-session-alive`; the only "one reader" sentence in `spec/` is
`ledger.als:27`, about `alloy-check`.

**The scope is wider than liveness.** Three scripts now hold rules that prose
elsewhere restates or could restate — `campaign-repos`, `campaign-settlement`,
`campaign-local-work` — and `campaign-settlement`'s header already says in words
that a second implementation of its reading would drift. So the thing to build is
one authoring-side check, not one guard per script.

The work:

1. Decide what the check reads. A candidate: a grep-based guard that fails when a
   tracked file outside `scripts/` contains a hand-rolled form of a rule a script
   owns — `ps -o comm=`/`ucomm` against a literal, a `## Repos` parse, a
   settled/closable verdict. Name the forms explicitly; a check that tries to
   recognise "a reading" in general will either miss everything or fire on prose
   that quotes the retired form on purpose, which `AGENTS.md` now does
   deliberately.
2. Decide where it runs. A `pre-commit` guard is the shape this machine already
   uses for the no-direct-commits rule.
3. State, beside each script that owns a rule, that the guard is its second
   reader — so the next person removing the guard sees what it was for.

The honest empty outcome passes: if the sweep shows no rule a script owns is
restated anywhere outside it, report that with the evidence and close this
without building a guard. What must not happen is the claim standing in
`AGENTS.md` with nothing behind it.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, where it was named and deferred rather
than filed — which `AGENTS.md` § Running a campaign forbids, since a finding
parked in a report reaches the close as nothing at all.

Done when either the guard is merged and

`scripts/campaign-session-alive`, and that the comparison must never be
hand-rolled. Nothing enforces it.

stays true only while a second reader enforces it, a validator or hook on the
authoring side. With the consumer as its only reader, the contract drifts exactly
like the hardcoded copy it replaced.* The four hand-rolled copies #65 removes are
what that drift looks like when it has already happened — they were four prose
copies of one test, and they were all wrong together.

`campaign-session-alive`; the only "one reader" sentence in `spec/` is

elsewhere restates or could restate — `campaign-repos`, `campaign-settlement`,
`campaign-local-work` — and `campaign-settlement`'s header already says in words

one authoring-side check, not one guard per script.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#61

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`
plan_items: `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.
issue.title: Name a session campaign-<anchor>-<role>-<n>, and retire the branch-as-name rule

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

## What is wrong

`campaign-1/80-phase2-sweep` (#80, PR #94) adds a third merge condition — the branch contains the current `main` at the moment it merges. Its chain survives attack. **Nothing enforces it.**

The owner authorised branch protection on `main` to fix that, and it was applied:

```
required_status_checks: { strict: true, contexts: [] }
enforce_admins: true
allow_force_pushes: false
allow_deletions: false
```

**Measured, and it enforces nothing.** A throwaway branch one commit behind `main` (#96, closed and deleted) read `mergeable=MERGEABLE`, `mergeStateStatus=CLEAN`, twice several seconds apart, with `behind=1 ahead=1`. "Require branches to be up to date" is a *modifier on required status checks*, and with `contexts: []` there is nothing for it to modify. The setting stores, reads back `strict=true`, and does nothing.

That is a sharper fact than an absent setting, and it is exactly the failure this campaign keeps meeting: a claimed reader that does not read. The force-push and deletion blocks **are** real.

## The work

Add one GitHub Actions workflow running the checks this repository already owns, and register it as a required status check so `strict` has something to be strict about.

- `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.
- `scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

**Ordering matters and is the part to get right.** A required check that no open pull request can produce blocks every merge. So: land the workflow first, watch it run green on a real pull request, and only then add its context to `required_status_checks.contexts`. Two pull requests are open while this lands.

Second-order benefit, and arguably the larger one: the guard and the model stop depending on a person remembering to run them. Today `alloy-check` is run because a rule says to.

## Done when

The pull request is merged, the workflow has run green on it, `contexts` names it, and a branch deliberately left behind `main` is refused — demonstrated the same way the current setting was falsified, not argued from the settings page.

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

Observed 2026-09-02 on #116: the stood-down delegate (`campaign-116-executor-1`), asked by the owner what was left, read `campaign-tracker settlement 116`, saw #119 `open`, and offered to take it — while `campaign-116-executor-2` was already running its `rm -rf`. No double execution happened (the offer was never accepted), but the only thing that prevented it was the owner not saying yes.

## Five whys

1. **Why did executor-1 offer a subtask already in progress?** Nothing it could read said so. Settlement shows `open`/`complete`/`dropped`; `runtime/claims/` held records for dotclaude#1 and #2 only; no branch existed for #119.
2. **Why was there no claim record for #119?** Executor-2 did #117, #118, #119, #123 and #124 with its own hands and subagents and never ran `campaign-claim take` for any of them.
3. **Why skip it?** For local-only work the claim is a branch on the container with nothing to commit to it, released afterward only with `--confirmed-absent`; the ceremony outweighed a three-command job, and both skills place the `take` step inside the file-then-brief-a-delegate flow, so the own-hands path never meets it.
4. **Why did nothing catch the skip?** No reader: `campaign-tracker settlement` reads issue state only, `campaign-claim live` reads records that exist, and an open issue with no record reads exactly like one not started. Absence passes — the shape `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` § Design names as the one that "gets trusted for months while enforcing nothing".
5. **Why is the design like that?** The claim was designed as branch = workspace for repository work (`agent.als` R4), and local work got "claim on the container all the same" as a prose rule (`AGENTS.md` § The `## Repos` list) with no consumer. A rule stated once in prose with no reader drifts, and it did — in the campaign whose author wrote the rule.

The delegate's own retrospective names a second, behavioural cause — a stood-down session re-entering as an executor without telling the launcher, and reporting a moving settlement as a snapshot (it had read #124 flip open → dropped between two reads and ignored the delta). Both hold; this issue is the structural one, since the behavioural one has no mechanism either.

Campaign: kalaluthien/campaign-base#1
Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

#176 made the branch ref the whole claim. That works for one repository and one shape of sub-issue. Four questions it left open were found by review on PR #183 (rounds three and four) and are deferred here rather than fixed there, because they are one design and not four fixes: PR #183's own record is that fixing them piecemeal produced a new stratum of defects each round.

Absorbs #186, which is question 1 stated narrowly.

## The design, before any code

Each of these gets a rule in `spec/campaign/` with a scenario that reddens when the rule is removed, and only then a script change.

**1. Claim identity across repositories.** `Claimed` is a set over `Issue`, so the model says a claim is per sub-issue. The script keys it by branch NAME and reads a repository list derived from the clones on disk, which gives three defects at once: `take` sweeps and re-checks on `--repo` only, so two takers with different `--repo` both claim the same sub-issue; `all_refs` collapses a same-named ref in a second repository, so `release` can delete the wrong one; and a member repository named in `## Repos` but not cloned here is unread while `live` prints that all readings were made. Decide what a claim's identity IS — the sub-issue, the (repository, branch) pair, or the sub-issue's own `repo` field — and make the readers agree with the model.

Also here, from PR #184's audit (N2): the model reads a claim over `claimedIssues` and has no `checkedOut` derivation, so a prunable-worktree scenario cannot discriminate from `R4h`. Whatever identity this question settles, derive the worktree reading (`checkedOut`) from it in the model, or record why the model stops above it.

**2. Release and close for a sub-issue whose ref never gains a commit.** `take --local` is gone, so a sub-issue whose work lives only under `<campaign>/scripts/` cuts a ref that stays level with `main`. `release` then refuses it as indistinguishable from a fresh claim, `--confirmed-absent` would be a false statement, and `closing-campaign` step 1 refuses on it. `spec/campaign/session/scenarios.als`'s `R4_RepolessCampaign` says exactly this campaign closes; the script at #183's head says it cannot. The issue's own `stateReason` is the unread fact that settles it.

Campaign: kalaluthien/campaign-base#1
Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

An executor that has just merged a sub-issue carries that sub-issue's whole transcript, and every turn of the next sub-issue re-reads it. `/compact` is the one thing that shrinks it, and nothing sends it. Two owner corrections on 2026-09-05 shaped what lands: compaction must fire the instant the executor is done, while that context is still in the prompt cache — run later it re-reads the whole transcript uncached and costs more than it saves; and the first draft's planner-side protocol and claim-ordering rule were too complex. One mechanism, at one moment.

Second: `AGENTS.md` states two channels in two sections with no criterion between them — § Delegate launch says a first brief arrives by `herdr agent prompt`, § The four messages says STATUS/REPORT/BLOCKED/STAND DOWN travel between sessions. A later assignment to a reused executor, the answer to a BLOCKED, and a slash command are undefined. That criterion belongs with this handoff, because both halves are the one handoff.

## What lands

1. **`campaign-claim.py release` enqueues `/compact` into the releasing session's own pane**, as its last act: `HERDR_ENV=1 herdr agent prompt <own pane> "/compact"`. herdr queues a prompt against a working pane, so compaction fires the moment the release turn ends, on the context that turn just used. The script finds its own pane by joining its harness session id to `herdr agent list`, and prints what it read — session id, pane, the command sent. **When no row names this session it says so and releases anyway**: compaction is a cost rule, not a gate, and a missing row must be visible, never silent. It never prompts a pane that is not its own.
2. **`scripts/campaign-assign.py <pane> <sub-issue>` is the planner's only assignment path.** It checks the pane is idle and has compacted since its last release — reading the pane text for the compaction marker, could-not-look printed and never silent — then sends the one-sentence prompt naming the sub-issue.
3. **The channel rule, stated once**, as one paragraph in `AGENTS.md` § The four messages naming that script: *an instruction to a session is a prompt into its pane; information between sessions is one of the four messages.* So every assignment (first or later), the answer to a BLOCKED, and `/compact` are prompts; REPORT, BLOCKED, STATUS and STAND DOWN stay messages. A prompt is the session's own user turn — hooks apply, no relay caveat; a message i

- One rule for who merges, stated once and enforced by the guard: the planner by role, or the claim's worker.
- It holds for both the base and a member repository.
- `planner.md`, `worker.md` steps 7-9, `campaign-roles.py` and `check-campaign-claim.py` agree, with a guard case for each outcome.
- The fallback no longer licenses a merge by some unrelated claim.
issue.intent:
- planner.md step 9 says the planner merges on a worker's `REPORT`. `AGENTS.md` § Merge conditions says none of the three conditions names a role. `campaign-roles.py` gives a planner `gh issue` and `gh label` only.
- What the guard does with a planner's `gh pr merge` (`runtime/guard.log`, 2026-09-14):
  - 07:34:03 REFUSED: html-doc-planner-10, `gh pr merge 32 -R kalaluthien/dotclaude`. The reason: "no claim covering it in a checkout of kalaluthien/dotclaude" (the member rule from rule-check#389).
  - 07:34:15 allowed: rule-check-planner-10, `gh pr merge 439`. It passed only because a claim worktree stood under the base root (the unnarrowed fallback), so any claim on this machine would have licensed it.
- So a planner can merge a member repository's pull request only by accident, and cannot merge one at all. Reported by html-doc-planner-10, who handed pr 32's merge to its worker.
plan_items: First a `NOTE` comparing two options through two lenses (what a wrong merge costs; how many steps each moves):
A: the guard admits a planner's `gh pr merge` when the pull request's head is a claim of the planner's campaign;
B: the worker holding the claim merges on the planner's prompt, and planner.md step 9 says so.
Then stop for the planner's `DECISION` before any code.
The spec first: `spec/campaign/orchestration/` if a merge's actor is modelled there.

issue.definition_of_done:
- A session reading a large file is steered to a grep and a bounded range by something it must consume, not a third copy of the prose.
- A review subagent's diff read is exempt.
- The threshold and the exemption are each stated once, and the check prints what it read and which branch it took.
- A case for each outcome fails first, then passes: steered, exempt, small file.
- The prose copies point at the check, or go.
issue.intent:
- rule-check#429 measured reads at 35.5% of tool-result bytes (rule-check#412). Its option C, grep first and then a bounded range, served:
  - 7 of 7 runs at 9.1% of the bytes (experiment 4, issuecomment-5660485351);
  - 6 of 6 anchored runs at 2.3% (experiment 5, issuecomment-5660796247).
- Review reads scored lower, but every miss lay outside the text read, so a whole read would have missed them too.
- The owner, 2026-09-14: make C the rule for a session's reads, and keep review diffs read whole.
- The rule exists in prose already: `AGENTS.md` § Execution mode says "Read only the part of a file you need", and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` says so too. The bytes show it is not followed, so the prose alone does not hold.
plan_items: First a `NOTE` with options, each tied to the #429 numbers and judged by bytes saved and wrong answers risked:
a `PreToolUse` hook on `Read` with no range over N lines;
a line in the brief hook;
a `filing`-shaped rule in `~/.claude/`;
others.

issue.intent:
- `.claude/skills/herdr/SKILL.md` copies `herdr --skill` at v0.8.2; the installed herdr is 0.9.0 and its text differs in 7 places (`agent_prompt_stalled`, "do not blindly submit it again", `herdr machine`, three safety rules). Nothing reports the drift.
- Its description, "only when the user explicitly mentions Herdr", is never met by a planner launching a delegate; its name and body move with every herdr release.
- Owner, 2026-09-17: keep herdr's text and our knowledge both under `references/`, as guide and facts; the skill's name and body must not move with a herdr upgrade or an environment change.
plan_items: `git mv` the directory; write `guide.md`; rewrite `SKILL.md` as a catalogue: the need, the reference that answers it.
Add `scripts/check-herdr-guide.py` and its test beside the other checks in `pre-commit`; it skips, saying so, where `herdr` is absent.
Sweep inbound paths by hand from `grep -rn`, not `sed` over the tree.
Trigger test with `claude -p` from the worktree, the negative three times.
Off limits: `spec/`, and `launching.md` beyond its paths.

Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

A second session that arrives in the container root with a request that is a subtask of an open campaign — while another session on this machine already holds that campaign — is today told to "join" it, which makes it a second campaign session: it surveys, files, claims, launches, and may sync or close the anchor. Witnessed 2026-08-28: session `agent-workspace-51` filed and claimed #36 while `agent-workspace-3a` (the session running campaign #1) sat idle and learned nothing, because nothing in `AGENTS.md`, `opening-campaign`, or the protocol says a session can be an *executor*. The holding session can see the peer in `ListAgents` (liveness) but cannot tell which subtask it works or address it for STATUS, so its close gate and its retirement sweep are blind to it — the "several sessions × the protocol" gap named in #36.

The rule to add, and where it lands:

1. **AGENTS.md § Who is a campaign session.** A session whose request is a subtask of an open campaign, when `ListAgents` shows a peer session on this machine, becomes that subtask's **executor session**: it files the subtask (or takes the one it was given), claims the branch, announces the claim to the holding session, and from then on is an agent in the protocol — it answers STATUS, sends REPORT and BLOCKED, stops on STAND DOWN, and never surveys, syncs, or closes the anchor. The holding session is the peer the person named; when none was named, the announcement goes to every peer session and a peer that holds no campaign covering it ignores it. The executor keeps working the subtask the way any executor may (own hands, subagent on a worktree, or a delegate); what changes is only who it reports to.
2. **The protocol gains one message**, executor → campaign, sent once at claim: `CLAIMED <branch> <ListAgents name>`. issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`closing-campaign` step 5 releases every `campaign-<N>/` ref still sitting at
`origin/main`, and it reads them with

```sh
gh api "repos/kalaluthien/agent-workspace/git/matching-refs/heads/campaign-$N/"
```

with **no `--paginate`**. GitHub pages that endpoint at thirty, so a campaign
with more than thirty branches gets a truncated list — and a truncated list of
refs reads exactly like a complete one, which is the sentence `AGENTS.md` already
uses about the sub-issue index two hundred lines earlier.

The consequence is quiet rather than destructive: refs past the first page are
never released, so claims outlive their campaign and the next campaign meets
branches nobody can explain. Nothing errors and the close reports success.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, which bounded five `gh issue list` surveys
on the same argument. This is the same class in the one place that reads refs
rather than issues, and it was not in #65's scope.

The work: add `--paginate`, and check whether any other `gh api` call in the two
skills or in `scripts/` reads a paged endpoint without it. `AGENTS.md:434`,
`opening-campaign/SKILL.md:332`, `docs/campaign-lifecycle.html:209` and
`scripts/campaign-settlement:86` were all verified paginated on 2026-08-30, so
the sweep is small.

Done when the pull request is merged, and the sweep's result is stated — the
fixed call, plus the list of `gh api` calls checked and found already correct.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

`AGENTS.md` will say, once #65 lands, that **liveness has one reader**,
`scripts/campaign-session-alive`, and that the comparison must never be
hand-rolled. Nothing enforces it.

This repository's own rule, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` § Design: *a declared contract
stays true only while a second reader enforces it, a validator or hook on the
authoring side. With the consumer as its only reader, the contract drifts exactly
like the hardcoded copy it replaced.* The four hand-rolled copies #65 removes are
what that drift looks like when it has already happened — they were four prose
copies of one test, and they were all wrong together.

Verified 2026-08-30: nothing under `spec/` or `docs/` mentions
`campaign-session-alive`; the only "one reader" sentence in `spec/` is
`ledger.als:27`, about `alloy-check`.

**The scope is wider than liveness.** Three scripts now hold rules that prose
elsewhere restates or could restate — `campaign-repos`, `campaign-settlement`,
`campaign-local-work` — and `campaign-settlement`'s header already says in words
that a second implementation of its reading would drift. So the thing to build is
one authoring-side check, not one guard per script.

The work:

1. Decide what the check reads. A candidate: a grep-based guard that fails when a
   tracked file outside `scripts/` contains a hand-rolled form of a rule a script
   owns — `ps -o comm=`/`ucomm` against a literal, a `## Repos` parse, a
   settled/closable verdict. Name the forms explicitly; a check that tries to
   recognise "a reading" in general will either miss everything or fire on prose
   that quotes the retired form on purpose, which `AGENTS.md` now does
   deliberately.
2. Decide where it runs. A `pre-commit` guard is the shape this machine already
   uses for the no-direct-commits rule.
3. State, beside each script that owns a rule, that the guard is its second
   reader — so the next person removing the guard sees what it was for.

The honest empty outcome passes: if the sweep shows no rule a script owns is
restated anywhere outside it, report that with the evidence and close this
without building a guard. What must not happen is the claim standing in
`AGENTS.md` with nothing behind it.

Found while verifying #65's fix round, where it was named and deferred rather
than filed — which `AGENTS.md` § Running a campaign forbids, since a finding
parked in a report reaches the close as nothing at all.

Done when either the guard is merged and

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#61

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`
plan_items: `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.
issue.title: Name a session campaign-<anchor>-<role>-<n>, and retire the branch-as-name rule

**Moved from #1 to #61 on the owner's word, 2026-08-30, after it had landed.** The naming rule is a herdr fact before it is a campaign rule: a session's two names are a herdr pane name and a harness name, both set through `herdr agent prompt` and `herdr agent rename`, and the deliverable is `scripts/campaign-name-session` — which is #61's Scope in its own words, *"`scripts/` — where a herdr recipe becomes a reader, in the shape `campaign-settlement` and `campaign-repos` already set."* The `AGENTS.md` section it added states that rule for a reader; it is not campaign machinery that would stand without herdr underneath it.

Owner instruction, 2026-08-30: the current naming is wrong in two ways. A delegate is named its branch with the slash flattened (`campaign-1-31-executor-identity`), and a campaign session keeps whatever the harness gave it. Neither says what the session *is*, and the campaign number leads a name that mostly is not the interesting part — a session that works only one campaign is the occasional case, not the normal one.

## The rule

```
campaign-<anchor>[-<issue>]-<role>
```

- `<anchor>` is the campaign's anchor issue number, always present — the campaign is what a session belongs to for as long as it runs.
- `<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
- `<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.

```
campaign-1-holder            holds campaign #1
campaign-1-80-executor       works subtask #80 of campaign #1
campaign-1-82-reviewer       reviews the pull request for subtask #82
```

**The anchor leads because it is the part that lasts** (owner, 2026-08-30). Subtasks keep arriving for as long as a campaign runs — that is what a campaign is — so leading with the subtask would lead with the field that turns over fastest, and `campaign-80-` reads as "campaign 80" for something that is not a campaign.

**A delegate is an executor** and gets no role word of its own (owner, 2026-08-30): where it runs changes how it is launched and how its liveness is read, not what it is doing. A subtask has one claim and a claim has one holder, so the name cannot collide.

It replaces the delegate rule — a delegate is `--name`d `campaign-<anchor>-<issue>-executor` rather than its flattened branch — so there is **one** naming rule instead of two.

## Both names, every time

A session has two names and they do not propagate to each other, measured 2026-08-30:

`

`<issue>` is the subtask, present only when the session is on one. A holder is not, so it has none.
`<role>` is `holder`, `executor`, or `reviewer`.
issue.title: Name a session campaign-<anchor>-<role>-<n>, and retire the branch-as-name rule

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

## What is wrong

`campaign-1/80-phase2-sweep` (#80, PR #94) adds a third merge condition — the branch contains the current `main` at the moment it merges. Its chain survives attack. **Nothing enforces it.**

The owner authorised branch protection on `main` to fix that, and it was applied:

```
required_status_checks: { strict: true, contexts: [] }
enforce_admins: true
allow_force_pushes: false
allow_deletions: false
```

**Measured, and it enforces nothing.** A throwaway branch one commit behind `main` (#96, closed and deleted) read `mergeable=MERGEABLE`, `mergeStateStatus=CLEAN`, twice several seconds apart, with `behind=1 ahead=1`. "Require branches to be up to date" is a *modifier on required status checks*, and with `contexts: []` there is nothing for it to modify. The setting stores, reads back `strict=true`, and does nothing.

That is a sharper fact than an absent setting, and it is exactly the failure this campaign keeps meeting: a claimed reader that does not read. The force-push and deletion blocks **are** real.

## The work

Add one GitHub Actions workflow running the checks this repository already owns, and register it as a required status check so `strict` has something to be strict about.

- `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.
- `scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

**Ordering matters and is the part to get right.** A required check that no open pull request can produce blocks every merge. So: land the workflow first, watch it run green on a real pull request, and only then add its context to `required_status_checks.contexts`. Two pull requests are open while this lands.

Second-order benefit, and arguably the larger one: the guard and the model stop depending on a person remembering to run them. Today `alloy-check` is run because a rule says to.

## Done when

The pull request is merged, the workflow has run green on it, `contexts` names it, and a branch deliberately left behind `main` is refused — demonstrated the same way the current setting was falsified, not argued from the settings page.
plan_items: `scripts/check-rule-readers` and `scripts/check-rule-readers-test` — pure Python 3, no dependencies.

`scripts/alloy-check` on all four modules under `spec/alloy/`. Feasible: `org.alloytools.alloy.dist.jar` is a stable release asset at `AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy` `v6.2.0`, byte-identical in size to the jar this machine runs (21062377), so CI fetches the same build rather than an approximation.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/agent-workspace#1

Observed 2026-09-02 on #116: the stood-down delegate (`campaign-116-executor-1`), asked by the owner what was left, read `campaign-tracker settlement 116`, saw #119 `open`, and offered to take it — while `campaign-116-executor-2` was already running its `rm -rf`. No double execution happened (the offer was never accepted), but the only thing that prevented it was the owner not saying yes.

## Five whys

1. **Why did executor-1 offer a subtask already in progress?** Nothing it could read said so. Settlement shows `open`/`complete`/`dropped`; `runtime/claims/` held records for dotclaude#1 and #2 only; no branch existed for #119.
2. **Why was there no claim record for #119?** Executor-2 did #117, #118, #119, #123 and #124 with its own hands and subagents and never ran `campaign-claim take` for any of them.
3. **Why skip it?** For local-only work the claim is a branch on the container with nothing to commit to it, released afterward only with `--confirmed-absent`; the ceremony outweighed a three-command job, and both skills place the `take` step inside the file-then-brief-a-delegate flow, so the own-hands path never meets it.
4. **Why did nothing catch the skip?** No reader: `campaign-tracker settlement` reads issue state only, `campaign-claim live` reads records that exist, and an open issue with no record reads exactly like one not started. Absence passes — the shape `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` § Design names as the one that "gets trusted for months while enforcing nothing".
5. **Why is the design like that?** The claim was designed as branch = workspace for repository work (`agent.als` R4), and local work got "claim on the container all the same" as a prose rule (`AGENTS.md` § The `## Repos` list) with no consumer. A rule stated once in prose with no reader drifts, and it did — in the campaign whose author wrote the rule.

The delegate's own retrospective names a second, behavioural cause — a stood-down session re-entering as an executor without telling the launcher, and reporting a moving settlement as a snapshot (it had read #124 flip open → dropped between two reads and ignored the delta). Both hold; this issue is the structural one, since the behavioural one has no mechanism either.

No double execution happened (the offer was never accepted), but the only thing that prevented it was the owner not saying yes.

## Five whys

1. **Why did executor-1 offer a subtask already in progress?** Nothing it could read said so. Settlement shows `open`/`complete`/`dropped`; `runtime/claims/` held records for dotclaude#1 and #2 only; no branch existed for #119.
2. **Why was there no claim record for #119?** Executor-2 did #117, #118, #119, #123 and #124 with its own hands and subagents and never ran `campaign-claim take` for any of them.
3. **Why skip it?** For local-only work the claim is a branch on the container with nothing to commit to it, released afterward only with `--confirmed-absent`; the ceremony outweighed a three-command job, and both skills place the `take` step inside the file-then-brief-a-delegate flow, so the own-hands path never meets it.

issue.body:
Campaign: kalaluthien/campaign-base#1
Repository: kalaluthien/campaign-base

#176 made the branch ref the whole claim. That works for one repository and one shape of sub-issue. Four questions it left open were found by review on PR #183 (rounds three and four) and are deferred here rather than fixed there, because they are one design and not four fixes: PR #183's own record is that fixing them piecemeal produced a new stratum of defects each round.

Absorbs #186, which is question 1 stated narrowly.

## The design, before any code

Each of these gets a rule in `spec/campaign/` with a scenario that reddens when the rule is removed, and only then a script change.

**1. Claim identity across repositories.** `Claimed` is a set over `Issue`, so the model says a claim is per sub-issue. The script keys it by branch NAME and reads a repository list derived from the clones on disk, which gives three defects at once: `take` sweeps and re-checks on `--repo` only, so two takers with different `--repo` both claim the same sub-issue; `all_refs` collapses a same-named ref in a second repository, so `release` can delete the wrong one; and a member repository named in `## Repos` but not cloned here is unread while `live` prints that all readings were made. Decide what a claim's identity IS — the sub-issue, the (repository, branch) pair, or the sub-issue's own `repo` field — and make the readers agree with the model.

Also here, from PR #184's audit (N2): the model reads a claim over `claimedIssues` and has no `checkedOut` derivation, so a prunable-worktree scenario cannot discriminate from `R4h`. Whatever identity this question settles, derive the worktree reading (`checkedOut`) from it in the model, or record why the model stops above it.

**2. Release and close for a sub-issue whose ref never gains a commit.** `take --local` is gone, so a sub-issue whose work lives only under `<campaign>/scripts/` cuts a ref that stays level with `main`. `release` then refuses it as indistinguishable from a fresh claim, `--confirmed-absent` would be a false statement, and `closing-campaign` step 1 refuses on it. `spec/campaign/session/scenarios.als`'s `R4_RepolessCampaign` says exactly this campaign closes; the script at #183's head says it cannot. The issue's own `stateReason` is the unread fact that settles it.
